interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the solid sum of sines square up into the rectifier's current block, and THD climb to 31%, when you add the 5th, 7th and higher harmonics one by one.
interactive.title: The six-pulse current taken apart
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Fourteen small screens on three cards, Harmonics, After isolation and Leakage. Each card shows only its own controls and readout.

Harmonics. The top plot shows one cycle of the current in one line of a six-pulse bridge. It is drawn as a dashed ideal block. A large coil in the DC link, chosen, holds the DC current steady. Each line conducts forward for 120°, rests for 60°, conducts backward for 120° and rests again. The block's height is the DC current, drawn as 1. A picker, Sines added, has eight settings. The first is Fundamental only and the last is Every harmonic. The picker's ends read Fundamental and Every one. Between them come Up to the 5th, Up to the 7th, Up to the 11th, Up to the 13th, Up to the 17th and Up to the 19th. The solid line is the sum of the sines added. The fundamental runs at the supply frequency. Its peak is 1.10 times the block's height, 2√3 ÷ π. Each harmonic h runs at h times the supply frequency. It is 1/h as tall as the fundamental, with the sign the block needs. These are the block's exact Fourier sines. With Every harmonic the sum is the block.

Below, a spectrum shows a bar for each harmonic added, as a share of the fundamental. The 5th is 20%, the 7th 14.3%, the 11th 9.1%, the 13th 7.7%, the 17th 5.9% and the 19th 5.3%. Empty slots stand at the even orders and the multiples of 3. A switch, 50 Hz or 60 Hz, relabels the bars in hertz. The readout, THD of the sum, is the root of the added harmonics' squares over the fundamental. In order it reads 0%, 20%, 25%, 26%, 27%, 28%, 28% and 31%. Beside it, three range bars show the current THD of real drives. A 6-pulse drive draws 25% to 40%, a 12-pulse one 9% to 11% and an 18-pulse one 3% to 4%.

After isolation. DC link voltage against time since isolation. Both drives start at 540 V. That is about what a three-phase bridge gives from 400 V, 1.35 × 400 V.[^1] Each drains through a 27 kΩ bleed resistor, chosen. Drive A has 2200 µF and drive B 6600 µF, both chosen. Each follows V = 540 × e^(−t ÷ RC). Drive A's RC is 59 s, about 1 minute. Drive B's is 178 s, about 3 minutes. Each curve has a dotted mark at about five time constants, at 5 and 15 minutes. Both marks show about 3 V. A time slider runs from 0 to 20 minutes in steps of 0.5 minutes. A picker chooses Drive A or Drive B. The readout is the chosen drive's link voltage then.

Leakage. A 400 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a drive. The drive's EMC filter sits at its input. It is three 100 nF capacitors, chosen, one from each line to a point bonded to earth. Each capacitor's reactance is X_C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 100 nF) = 31.8 kΩ. A small phasor diagram shows each capacitor's current and their sum. The sum is the readout, the current through earth. A picker, Case, has five settings.

Earthed, balanced. The supply's star point is earthed, and the three lines pass through an RCD, drawn as a ring. Each line is 230 V from earth, so each capacitor passes 230 ÷ 31.8 kΩ = 7.2 mA. The three are 120° apart and add to 0 mA. Earthed, a phase lost. L1's fuse has blown, and its capacitor carries nothing. The other two, 120° apart, add to 7.2 mA. It returns through earth to the star point, outside the RCD's ring. So the RCD sees it.

Insulated, healthy. The star point is not earthed. An insulation monitor sits between the system and earth. Each capacitor still passes 7.2 mA. With no path back from earth, the three only circulate among the lines. The current through earth is 0 mA. The filter carries a label: Disconnect on an insulated supply. Insulated, L1 earth fault. A red link joins L1 to earth. The L2 and L3 capacitors now each see about 400 V, √3 × 230 V. Each passes 12.5 mA. Their currents are 60° apart and add to 21.7 mA, three capacitors' worth. That current flows through the fault, drawn red. Insulated, fault, filter out. The filter is disconnected, and the fault draws almost nothing, drawn as 0 mA. In both fault cases the monitor's alarm lamp lights.

Three readouts sit in a row. They are free to wrap onto two lines on a narrow phone. Under the picture on each show screen, a Play again button replays its demonstration.

The screens. Unless a screen says otherwise, the Harmonics card opens at 50 Hz.

1, show: Blocks from sines. Harmonics, Sines added going from Fundamental only to Up to the 7th. The words: “A six-pulse bridge with a large coil in its DC link draws a steady current. Each line carries it in blocks, 120° forward, a 60° rest, then 120° back. Any wave that repeats each cycle is a sum of sines. The fundamental is the sine at the supply frequency. The harmonics run at whole multiples of that frequency. In ideal blocks, harmonic h is 1/h as tall as the fundamental.” Read: with the fundamental, 5th and 7th added, the solid sum follows the dashed block. It still ripples at the corners. Still: Up to the 7th.

2, a puzzle: Harmonics at 60 Hz, Up to the 7th, the readout and the row of hertz hidden. “A drive on a 60 Hz supply draws a 60 A fundamental, in ideal blocks. What does its 5th harmonic carry?” Offered: “12 A at 300 Hz”; “12 A at 250 Hz”; “60 A at 300 Hz”. Hint for 250 Hz: “That is the 5th of 50 Hz. This supply runs at 60 Hz.” Hint for 60 A: “Each harmonic is 1/h as tall as the fundamental.” Why: “12 A at 300 Hz. The 5th runs at 5 × 60 = 300 Hz. In ideal blocks it is 1/5 of the fundamental, 60 ÷ 5 = 12 A. Real drives roughly follow this rule.[^2]” A right Check switches to Up to the 5th and shows the row of hertz. The 5th's bar then reads 300 Hz.

3, show: The gaps. Harmonics, Every harmonic. The words: “The bars stand only at the 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th, 17th and 19th. That is 6n ± 1, for any whole number n.[^3] There is no even harmonic. An even harmonic is the same in both half cycles. The block flips sign, so it cannot contain one. There is no multiple of 3 either. Those are in step in all three lines and need a neutral to return. A bridge has none. The 5th and 7th are the biggest.[^4]” Read: the spectrum has bars at 5, 7, 11, 13, 17 and 19. The slots at the even orders and the multiples of 3 stand empty.

4, a puzzle: Harmonics, Every harmonic. “Which of these could a six-pulse bridge draw from a 50 Hz supply?” Offered: “The 9th, at 450 Hz”; “The 11th, at 550 Hz”; “The 10th, at 500 Hz”. Hint for the 9th: “9 is a multiple of 3. Where would it return?” Hint for the 10th: “An even harmonic is the same in both half cycles. The block flips sign.” Why: “The 11th, since 11 = 6 × 2 − 1. The 9th would be in step in all three lines, with no neutral to carry it. The 10th is even, so it is the same in both half cycles. The block flips sign, so it holds none.” A right Check marks the 11th's bar, 550 Hz.

5, show: One number, THD. Harmonics, Sines added going from Fundamental only to Every harmonic. The words: “Total harmonic distortion, THD, puts one number on the harmonics. It is their combined rms over the fundamental's rms.[^5] Sines of different frequencies add as squares. So THD = √(I5² + I7² + …) ÷ I1. Perfect blocks give 31%. Real six-pulse drives often draw 25% to 40%.[^6] A twelve-pulse rectifier feeds two bridges out of step, so their 5th and 7th cancel. It draws 9% to 11%. Eighteen-pulse ones cancel more and draw 3% to 4%.” Read: as the sines are added, THD climbs from 0% to 31%. Beside it, the bar for real 6-pulse drives reads 25% to 40%. The 12-pulse bar reads 9% to 11%, and the 18-pulse bar 3% to 4%. Still: Every harmonic.

6, a puzzle: Harmonics, Up to the 7th, the readout hidden. “Only the 5th and 7th are present, at 1/5 and 1/7 of the fundamental. What is the THD?” Offered: “About 34%, the two added”; “About 6%, their squares added”; “About 25%”. Hint for 34%: “Different frequencies do not add straight. They add as squares.” Hint for 6%: “You added the squares. Now take the root.” Why: “About 25%. The 5th is 20% and the 7th 14.3%. Two sines of different frequencies multiply to an average of zero. So only their squares add. √(0.20² + 0.143²) = √0.0604, about 0.25.” A right Check shows the readout, 25%.

7, show: Charge after isolation. After isolation, Drive A, the time slider going from 0 to 5 minutes. The words: “Isolation stops the supply. It does not empty the DC link. A bleed resistor across the link drains it on the RC curve, V = 540 × e^(−t ÷ RC). Drive A's RC is about 1 minute. In 5 minutes, about five time constants, it falls to about 3 V. Drive B has three times the capacitance, so it takes about 15 minutes. Each drive has its own wait.” Read: drive A's link falls from 540 V to about 3 V at 5 minutes. Drive B's curve is still near 100 V there. It reaches about 3 V near 15 minutes. Still: Drive A, 5 minutes.

8, a puzzle: After isolation, Drive B, time 5 minutes, the readout hidden. “Drive B is isolated, and its display is dark. You have waited 5 minutes, drive A's time. What is its link at?” Offered: “Nothing, as the display is dark”; “About 3 V, like drive A”; “About 100 V”. Hint for nothing: “The display runs from a control supply. The link drains on its own curve.” Hint for 3 V: “Drive B's time constant is three times drive A's.” Why: “About 100 V. Drive B's RC is 178 s. So 540 × e^(−300 ÷ 178) is about 100 V. High voltage can be present while an indicator is dark.[^7] So wait the time given for that drive, then measure the link.[^8]” A right Check shows the readout, 100 V.

9, show: Leakage that cancels. Leakage, the case going from Earthed, balanced to Earthed, a phase lost. The words: “A drive's EMC filter puts a small capacitor from each line to earth. With 100 nF on 230 V at 50 Hz, X_C is 31.8 kΩ. So each passes 7.2 mA. The three currents are 120° apart, so they cancel. Lose a phase, and the two left no longer cancel. Their sum, 7.2 mA, returns through earth, so the RCD sees it.” Read: balanced, the three 7.2 mA phasors add to 0 mA through earth. With L1 lost, two phasors 120° apart add to 7.2 mA. The RCD sees it. Still: Earthed, a phase lost.

10, a puzzle: Leakage, Earthed, balanced, the readout hidden. “The filter sends nothing to earth while the supply is balanced. Then one supply fuse blows. What flows through earth now?” Offered: “Still nothing”; “About 7.2 mA”; “About 21.7 mA, all three added”. Hint for nothing: “Two currents 120° apart. Do they cancel on their own?” Hint for 21.7 mA: “The lost line's capacitor carries nothing.” Why: “About 7.2 mA. Two equal phasors 120° apart add to one of the same size. So the earth current jumps from nothing to 7.2 mA. The RCD sees all of it.” A right Check sets Earthed, a phase lost.

11, show: The insulated supply. Leakage, the case going from Insulated, healthy to Insulated, L1 earth fault, then Insulated, fault, filter out. The words: “Now the supply's star point is not earthed. No wire joins earth back to the supply. So a first earth fault draws almost nothing.[^9] The filter spoils that. Fault L1 to earth, and the L2 and L3 capacitors see about 400 V. Each passes 12.5 mA, and the two are 60° apart. Together they draw 21.7 mA through the fault, three capacitors' worth. So on an insulated supply the filter is disconnected.[^10]” Read: with the filter in, a fault on L1 carries 21.7 mA. With the filter out, the same fault draws almost nothing. Still: Insulated, L1 earth fault.

12, a mixed puzzle: Leakage, Insulated, healthy. “A drive is fitted on an insulated supply. The insulation monitor alarms each time the drive is switched on, then settles. What is the likeliest cause?” Offered: “The motor has an earth fault”; “Its EMC filter is still connected”; “The DC link kept its charge”. Hint for the motor: “A winding fault would not clear a moment later.” Hint for the DC link: “A charged link would be there before switch-on, not only at it.” Why: “Its EMC filter is still connected. The monitor watches the whole connected circuit, drive included.[^11] It reads any current between the system and earth as failing insulation. At each switch-on, the filter's capacitors charge through it. So the monitor alarms.[^12] The filter would also give a real fault a return path. So disconnect it, as the drive's instructions require.[^10]” A right Check lights the filter's label, Disconnect on an insulated supply.

13, a mixed puzzle: Leakage, Earthed, balanced, the readout hidden throughout. “A fault inside a three-phase drive, on its DC link, sends DC with little ripple to earth. An RCD protects the circuit against shock. Which type?” Offered: “Type A”; “Type AC”; “Type B”. Hint for Type A: “Type A sees sine AC and pulsating DC. Is this DC pulsing?” Hint for Type AC: “Type AC is only for loads with no DC in their current.” Why: “Type B. Type A detects only sinusoidal AC and pulsating DC.[^13] DC from the link barely pulses. For shock protection, a three-phase drive's maker may allow only Type B.[^14] Regulation 531.3.3 of BS 7671 sets out the types.[^15]” A right Check labels the RCD Type B.

14, a mixed puzzle: Harmonics, Every harmonic. “Three single-phase rectifier loads share a four-wire supply, one on each line. Each line carries a 10 A 3rd harmonic. What does the neutral carry at 150 Hz?” Offered: “Nothing”; “10 A”; “30 A”. Each wrong pick's hint points to the 3rds being in step. Why: a 120° shift is 360° at three times the frequency, so the 3rds add, 3 × 10 = 30 A, and a bridge with no neutral draws none. A right Check rings the empty slot at the 3rd, labelled no 3rd.

Each puzzle offers three answers, stacked, each free to wrap. A wrong pick gets its hint. Why? explains. Continue moves on.
interactive.ignores: The blocks are ideal, with square corners and a perfectly steady DC current. Real ones have sloped edges. The current takes time to pass from one diode to the next. Without a large coil, the capacitor makes a drive draw two gulps each half cycle. Those gulps carry harmonics too. The supply is drawn as a perfect sine. In truth, harmonic currents bend it a little. Phase-shifting transformers let 12 and 18-pulse rectifiers cancel harmonics. That is left for Transformers. The discharge curves use one bleed resistor and nothing else. Real links also drain into control circuits. A failed bleed resistor can leave the charge there far longer. The filter is three plain capacitors. Real filters also pass high-frequency current from the switching. They are never perfectly balanced, either. With a phase lost, the lost line is drawn carrying nothing. In a real drive it floats. The insulated supply's own cable capacitance to earth is left out. So its fault currents read zero rather than small. The EMC categories C1 to C4 and the filter's working band are left out.

explain.text:
Power electronics brings three side effects with it. A diode rectifier draws its current in blocks or pulses, not as a sine. That puts extra frequencies on the supply. A DC link stays charged after you isolate it. And a drive's input filter leaks current to earth.

Start with the current. A six-pulse bridge with a large coil in its DC link draws a steady current. Each line carries it in blocks, 120° forward and 120° back. That is because each line sits in two of the six 60° diode pairs each way. Any wave that repeats each cycle is a sum of sines at whole multiples of the supply frequency. These are its [[harmonics]]. The fundamental is the sine at the supply frequency. For ideal blocks, harmonic h is 1/h as tall as the fundamental. From a balanced supply, only the orders 6n ± 1 appear. Those are the 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th and on. Even ones cannot appear. An even harmonic is the same in both half cycles, but the block flips sign. Multiples of 3 cannot, because the three lines have no neutral to return them. [[Total harmonic distortion]], THD, is the harmonics' combined rms over the fundamental's rms. Sines of different frequencies multiply to an average of zero. So their rms values add as squares. Perfect blocks give 31%. Real six-pulse drives often draw 25% to 40%. These currents flow back through the generator and cables. Their reactance rises with frequency, so each harmonic current makes a harmonic voltage. That bends the voltage every other load sees. So ship rules cap a distribution system's voltage THD at 8%.[^16] It may go higher only if all its equipment is built and documented for more.

Isolation stops the supply, but it does not empty the DC link. A bleed resistor drains the link on the RC curve. So the drive's own R and C set the wait. One maker asks for 5 minutes. Another asks for at least 15.

An [[EMC filter]] limits how much of a drive's fast switching spreads back into the supply. For the least radio interference, also bond the motor cable's screen all round where it enters the motor's terminal box.[^20] The filter puts a small capacitor from each line to earth. Each one passes V ÷ X_C. On a balanced earthed supply, the three currents are 120° apart. So they cancel. Lose a phase, and two are left. Two equal currents 120° apart add to one of the same size. That current flows through earth, so the RCD sees it. A fault in a three-phase converter can also carry DC. Type B protects against that. Type A detects only sinusoidal AC and pulsating DC. An insulated supply has no planned path back from earth. So a first fault draws almost nothing. The filter would give that fault a return path. So it is disconnected. Most drives have a diode rectifier, a DC link and an EMC filter. So most bring these three effects with them. This picture is simplified. It uses ideal blocks, one bleed resistor and plain capacitors. **A converter draws harmonics, holds charge after isolation and leaks current to earth. So you measure, wait and choose the protection to suit.**

analogy.text: A drive's current works like a note on a guitar string. The string sounds its main pitch. Above it sound quieter overtones, at whole multiples of that pitch. The overtones give the note its shape. In the same way, the 5th, 7th and higher harmonics give the current its block shape. Take the overtones away and only a pure tone, a sine, is left.
analogy.breaks: A string makes its own overtones. Here the supply is a sine. The harmonics come from the load drawing current in blocks. And a string's overtones change with where it is plucked. A six-pulse bridge's are fixed by its blocks. Only orders 6n ± 1 appear, each about 1/h of the fundamental.

practice.text:
Safe isolation comes first. A drive can hold a lethal charge with its isolator off and its display dark.

- Isolate the drive, and any UPS battery or other supply to its DC link.
- Wait the discharge time printed for that drive. One maker asks for 5 minutes.[^17] Another asks for at least 15.[^8]
- Measure the DC link at its test points before you touch anything. A dark indicator proves nothing.
- On an earthed supply, fit the RCD type the drive's maker requires. For shock protection, a three-phase drive's maker may allow only Type B.[^14]
- On an insulated supply, disconnect the drive's EMC filter. Expect the insulation monitor to see the drive as part of the whole connected circuit.
- Measure harmonics with a power quality meter. THDI is the current's distortion. THDV is the voltage's.

**Rules of thumb:** each harmonic of a six-pulse drive is about the fundamental ÷ h. A reactor in a drive's supply limits its harmonic currents. Cheap filters can leak enough current to clash with an installation's safety rules. Some drives have a normal touch current over 3.5 mA AC. Their protective earth conductor's minimum size then follows the local rules for high protective conductor current.[^18] On a ship, regular harmonic measurements help catch a filter failing as it starts.

**Worked example:** a drive on an earthed 440 V, 60 Hz supply has 100 nF from each line to earth. Each line is 440 ÷ √3 = 254 V from earth. X_C = 1 ÷ (2π × 60 × 100 nF) = 26.5 kΩ. So each capacitor passes 254 ÷ 26.5 kΩ = 9.6 mA. Balanced, the three cancel. Lose a phase, and 9.6 mA flows to earth. Put 3 such drives on one RCD and lose the same phase to all of them. Then 28.7 mA flows through it. A 30 mA RCD may trip at anything from 15 mA up.[^19] So it would very likely trip. Two such drives, 19.1 mA, could trip it too.

**Common mistakes**
- Blaming harmonics on the supply. They come from the load drawing its current in blocks.
- Adding THD figures straight. Harmonics add as squares.
- Taking a dark display or an open isolator as a dead DC link.
- Using one discharge time for every drive. Each drive's R and C set its own.
- Fitting a Type A or Type AC RCD where the drive's maker requires Type B.
- Leaving the EMC filter connected on an insulated supply.

applied.problem: Several claims are wider than true: every drive does not bring all three effects (low-harmonic IGBT front ends exist); filters limit, not stop, emissions; 6n±1 only holds for a balanced supply; six-pulse drives without chokes exceed 40%; the 8% ship limit is voltage THD and may be relaxed if docume…

The worked example puts drives on an RCD without saying the 440 V supply is earthed, contradicting the step to disconnect the filter on an insulated supply; the ship measurement point is about filter failure, and the 3.5 mA rule is about high protective conductor current.

At exactly five time constants the link is 540 × e^−5 = 3.6 V, not about 3 V; at 5 and 15 minutes it is 3.5 V, so tie the 3 V to those times. Screen 5 states the 25-40% range as true of every real six-pulse drive; ones without a choke draw more.
